chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halaby, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The Ihram is from five Mawaqit (stations of entering the state of Ihram) which the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) designated. It is not befitting for a pilgrim (Hajj) nor for a pilgrim (Umra) to enter Ihram before them, nor after them. He designated Dhul Huleifa for the people of Medina, and it is Masjid al-Shajara, where prayer is performed and Hajj is obligated therein. He designated Al-Juhfa for the people of Syria. He designated Al-Aqiq for the people of Najd. He designated Qaran al-Manazil for the people of Taif. He designated Yalamlam for the people of Yemen. And it is not befitting for anyone to turn away from the Mawaqit of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family).

key_terms.إِحْرَامٌ: The state of ritual consecration for Hajj or Umra
key_terms.الْجُحْفَةَ: Al-Juhfa, the Miqat for people of Syria
key_terms.الْعَقِيقَ: Al-Aqiq, the Miqat for people of Najd
key_terms.ذَا الْحُلَيْفَةِ: Dhul Huleifa, the Miqat for people of Medina
key_terms.قَرْنَ الْمَنَازِلِ: Qaran al-Manazil, the Miqat for people of Taif
key_terms.مَسْجِدُ الشَّجَرَةِ: Masjid al-Shajara, the location of Dhul Huleifa
key_terms.مَوَاقِيتَ: Designated stations or places for entering Ihram
key_terms.يَلَمْلَمَ: Yalamlam, the Miqat for people of Yemen

ai.seo_question: What are the five designated Mawaqit for Ihram in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi details the five specific Miqat stations established by the Prophet Muhammad for pilgrims from Medina, Syria, Najd, Taif, and Yemen, serving as the foundational legal boundaries for entering the state of Ihram. It underscores the binding nature of these locations, prohibiting entry into Ihram before or after them, which aligns with the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on adhering strictly to the Prophet's prescribed rituals. The mention of Dhat al-Hulayfah (Masjid al-Shajara) as the Miqat for Medinans highlights its historical significance as the primary starting point for the Prophet himself.
